card.title: ZCG and the dev fund
card.byline: Zcash forum threads on whether to end, shrink, restructure or redirect the Zcash Community Grants stream and treasury, and how Zcash development should be funded.

output.headline: Zcash forum debates ending, shrinking or reshaping ZCG and the development fund

overview.text: Six forum threads in late October 2026 argue over Zcash Community Grants (ZCG), the committee-run grants programme that receives 8% of block rewards and holds a treasury of roughly $100M or more; the opening proposal would end ZCG at NU8 and send its stream and remaining treasury to the Network Sustainability Mechanism (NSM).

Other proposals include ending only ZCG's stream, ending the whole development fund, ZCG's own taper plan, a Future Dev and Legal Defense Fund ZIP that would donate about $50M to the NSM, restructuring ZCG, and a Zcash Adoption Pool (ZAP) that would refocus the ZCG stream on adoption among people who need private money.

Those who want ZCG ended cite its lack of accountability to coinholders, spending against the ZSA poll and a treasury too large for a committee; those who want it kept cite the poll's advisory status, ZCG's record, unfinished work and the weaknesses of coinholder voting, and many ask that coinholder grants be treated alike.

The Future Dev and Legal Defense Fund ZIP has drawn support and offers to withdraw rival drafts, but also objections to its numbers, its legal fund and the pace of the process, and ZAP, posted on 31 October, opened a new argument over what adoption funding should pay for; no agreed way of deciding has emerged.

points.text: ZCG is paid for by diluting coinholders, yet its committee is chosen through ZCAP, a panel whose membership the Zcash Foundation decides and in which 36% of members have received ZCG grants, so those who pay have no say and those who are paid do: self-dealing and taxation without representation.

ZCG's decisions run against what holders want: it approved another $455K for ZSAs after 98.6% of coinholder votes cast were against them, it funded adult-industry events, and much of its funded work shows little adoption.

ZCG's treasury, now $100M or more, far exceeds what a committee built for under $10M can allocate well and its stream adds millions each week, so the stream should stop whatever ZCG's performance; ZCG had a month to propose its own answer and did not.

No committee can know what to fund, because that knowledge is spread across users and builders and shows in what they choose to pay for; donors, companies and crowdfunding can fill gaps as in Linux and Bitcoin, and anyone with capital can write a check today.

The ZSA poll was an advisory, non-binding NU7 sentiment poll, not a vote to halt the work, and its 98.6% is a share of participating coin weight on low turnout; the later grant was meant to preserve and integrate work already funded, so it does not show ZCG defied a mandate.

Zcash's work is not done and, with capital finally available, it should be deployed under experienced leadership and a long-term plan, not given away; private funding is scarce and will not reliably cover the community, research and new teams that grants have supported.

Coinholder voting is no safer than a committee: it is weighted by ZEC held, turnout is low, votes are anonymous and open to capture, and the ZCG slice belongs to ZCG under the protocol, so calling it 'our money' does not settle who should control it.

ZCG has a solid record: it funded light-wallet hosting, Ledger and Trezor support, Arti, payment and bridge integrations and security work, declines many proposals on cost, and has had few failures among hundreds of grants.

ZCG's problems are structural and fixable, so it should be restructured rather than dissolved: defined goals, sub-committees or grant tracks with accountable program managers, experienced leadership, or its treasury held under a legal trust.

Ending only ZCG's stream is a half-measure: coinholder-controlled grants raise the same objections, so either both streams end or neither does; some add that the fund has served its purpose, funding is no longer scarce, and it expires in 2028 anyway.

The ZCG and coinholder streams differ in kind, since holders vote on each coinholder grant while ZCG is a committee, so each should be decided separately rather than in one package; coinholder grants have funded high-signal security and infrastructure work.

Sending ZCG's stream and treasury to the NSM takes the money out of circulation and pays it to miners slowly over decades, with no committee or election to capture, and the NSM exists whatever happens to ZCG's stream.

Ending ZCG's stream without a development-focused replacement shifts money from development to miners: the NSM would not pay out until about 2031, it adds a second issuance curve, and some of those pressing for it are tied to mining.

A middle path beats abolition or the status quo: end or taper ZCG's inflow, donate part of its treasury to the NSM and keep a smaller grants capability, which FPF's counsel says can be done lawfully with a community vote and an accepted ZIP.

The compromises leave core objections open: the taper keeps ZCG funded to 2032 without fixing accountability, and the Future Dev and Legal Defense Fund ZIP's 55% donation is not derived from a goal, is fixed in ZEC with no dollar cap, and leaves the legal fund's role unclear.

Do not rush or take ZCG's holdings: there is no emergency, ZCG's funds are restricted under ZIP 1015 and reallocating them would take community money without approval; let the inflow stop if need be, and allow months of debate with better polling.

ZAP reaffirms what ZIP 1015 intended: grants that bring people who need private money, such as the debanked, sex workers, refugees and small businesses, onto shielded ZEC build real use, and the ZIP guarantees funding to no one.

Giving ZEC to recipients is unlikely to create lasting users, since many will cash out and airdrop retention is low, and Zcash is a currency, not a charity: contested social causes should not be paid from shared issuance, and any programme needs verifiable metrics first.

Hate has no place in Zcash: mocking people over the ZECsy grant for being trans or Jewish, or for who they try to reach, is unacceptable, silence reads as permission, and at-risk groups including the adult industry are legitimate users Zcash exists to serve.

Objecting to spending block-reward funds on adult-industry events or other contested causes is about public money, not identity: no one denies anyone the right to use Zcash, and reframing criticism of a grant as an attack on identity sidesteps that argument.

groupings.disclaimer: These groupings are approximate. Many people hold positions from more than one group, some changed their minds during the discussion, and nobody chose a side by being listed here.

groups.label: Ending ZCG's funding and treasury
groups.note: Points that start from accountability to coinholders, the size of the treasury and a preference for market-based funding.

groups.label: Keeping and defending ZCG
groups.note: Points that rest on the poll's advisory status, unfinished work, ZCG's record and the limits of coinholder voting.

groups.note: Points about restructuring ZCG, middle paths that cut its inflow and donate part of its treasury, and objections to taking its holdings.
